Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 183 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 98.6, target 99.5. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 11.3, target 9.0. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 27.9, target 29.4. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 0.0, target 7.2. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 3.6. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 10.8. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 1.8, target 12.8. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 1.1, target 1.1. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

When someone faces a hard decision, asking more than one person for advice can lead to a much better choice. Every person sees a problem through their own experiences, so one opinion is always limited.

For example, imagine a student deciding whether to join the soccer team or the school play. Her coach might push soccer because he knows her talent on the field. Her drama teacher might say the play will build her confidence. Her older brother, who did both, might warn her that practices for the two often overlap and that she will be exhausted. Each person gives her a piece of the picture, and together the pieces show her what really matters.

Multiple opinions also help catch mistakes. If one friend says a used car is a great deal, a second friend who knows engines might notice a leak the first person missed.

Finally, hearing different views forces a person to think for themselves. Instead of simply obeying one voice, they must weigh reasons and decide what fits their own life. That careful thinking is what makes a choice wise.
